source.title: Work, Wages, and Worth
source.summary: Labor markets, youth unemployment in MENA, female participation, brain drain, and Islamic labor ethics.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: Youth unemployment in the Middle East and North Africa is the highest in the world at 25 to 30 percent. Female labor force participation in many Muslim-majority countries is below 20 percent. Brain drain has cost countries like Pakistan hundreds of thousands of skilled professionals. These aren't problems caused by Islam. They're caused by governance failures and cultural norms sometimes falsely attributed to religion. The Islamic tradition has powerful things to say about labor: pay workers before their sweat dries, the prohibition of exploitation, the concept of ihsan (excellence) in work. But the gap between these principles and reality is vast. The kafala system in Gulf states, the informal economy employing 60 to 80 percent of workers without protections, the exclusion of women from economic participation. Closing that gap isn't just moral. It's economic. Countries that waste their human potential don't grow.
